AMIBINKD MANUAL
Native AmigaOS 3.x port of binkd, the FTN mailer
Version 10.31
===============================================================================

Author (Amiga port): Gary "Spitfire" McCulloch
Upstream project:     binkd (https://github.com/pgul/binkd)
Site:                 https://www.rofbbs.com
BBS:                  call.rofbbs.com:6800

This manual documents the AmigaOS-specific parts of AmiBinkD: what changed
from stock binkd, how to install and run it on a real or emulated Amiga,
the configuration keywords actually used in a working setup, and every
real-hardware behavioral quirk found while porting it. For a short
Aminet-style overview, see readme.txt.

This manual does NOT attempt to replace upstream binkd's own
documentation of the BinkP protocol, FTN packet format, or the full
config-file keyword list -- binkd has many keywords this port never
exercised and never needed to touch. Everywhere this manual is silent on
a keyword or behavior, assume it matches stock binkd.

===============================================================================
01. WHAT AMIBINKD DOES
===============================================================================

AmiBinkD sends and receives FTN (FidoNet Technology Network) mail over
TCP/IP using the BinkP protocol. It is the same job stock binkd does on
Unix/Windows/etc, cross-compiled and adapted to run natively on classic
AmigaOS 3.x -- no ixemul.library, no ixnet.library.

Outbound (client/poll mode, "-p -P<address>"):

1. Connects to the configured host:port for that node.
2. Performs the BinkP handshake (protocol/option negotiation, CRAM-MD5
   password authentication if a node password is configured).
3. Exchanges SYS/LOC/ZYZ/TIME/VER/BUILD system info with the remote.
4. Sends any mail/files queued in that domain's outbound directory.
5. Receives any mail/files the remote has queued for you.
6. Closes the session cleanly.

Inbound (server mode, "-s"):

1. Listens on the configured TCP port.
2. Accepts a connection, performs the same handshake, authenticates the
   remote against your configured node password (or accepts as
   non-secure if none is configured and send-if-pwd allows it).
3. Exchanges mail/files.
4. Returns to listening for the next connection.

Received files land in your configured inbound directory as standard
.pkt (packet) or file-echo files, ready for your tosser (e.g. C-Net/5's
Toss) to process. AmiBinkD itself does not parse message content -- it
only moves FTN transport-layer files.


===============================================================================
02. REQUIREMENTS
===============================================================================

* Commodore Amiga, real or emulated, AmigaOS 3.0 or newer (m68k)
* bsdsocket.library -- tested against Amiberry's bsdsocket_emu; should
  work against real Roadshow/AmiTCP but has not been verified there (see
  section 15 before assuming a finding applies beyond Amiberry)
* An FTN-aware BBS engine or tosser (built and tested against C-Net/5
  Amiga Pro; AmiBinkD itself is BBS-agnostic -- it only reads/writes
  standard FTN outbound-flow and packet files)
* At least one FTN address and a hub/uplink willing to carry your mail
* TCP/IP connectivity to that hub (a real or forwarded port for inbound)

AmiBinkD is a standalone compiled executable with no ixemul.library or
ixnet.library dependency of any kind.


===============================================================================
03. FILES INCLUDED
===============================================================================

The AmiBinkD package should include:

AmiBinkD                  Compiled AmigaOS executable (m68k, AmigaOS 3.0+)
AmiBinkD.info             Workbench icon (AmigaOS 3.5+ for the colour
                          image; older Workbench shows a generic one)
readme.txt                Short Aminet-style overview
manual.txt                This document
amibinkd-example.cfg      Example configuration file
amibinkd.scr              Example AmigaDOS poll-all driver script

Copy amibinkd-example.cfg to a config name of your choosing before
editing it -- see section 07 for whether you want one config file or
several.

amibinkd.scr is a ready-to-edit "-P ALL" poll script (see sections 07
and 09) -- point it at your own config name and schedule it from your
BBS's event/maintenance system.


===============================================================================
04. RECOMMENDED DIRECTORY LAYOUT
===============================================================================

A working setup looks like:

AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD              the executable
AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD.cfg          config used by the inbound server (-s)
AmiBinkD:<net>.cfg             one config per network, used for polling
AmiBinkD:<net>.scr             one small Execute script per network
SysData:log/<net>.log          one log per network (or a shared log)
DH3:Echomail/Outbound/         per-domain outbound flow files
DH3:Echomail/Inbound/          received packets/files land here
DH3:Echomail/Inbound_Temp/     in-progress receive staging

These paths match this port's own deployment (Reign of Fire BBS,
C-Net/5); adjust to your own system's assigns. What matters is that
every "domain" line's outbound directory, and the inbound/temp-inbound
directories, actually exist before you run AmiBinkD -- it does not
create them for you.


===============================================================================
05. CONCURRENCY -- MORE THAN ONE SESSION AT A TIME
===============================================================================

Through v10.4, this port ran every BinkP session synchronously, one at a
time -- classic AmigaOS has no fork()/pthreads without ixemul.library
(deliberately avoided here), so stock binkd's own "DOS" build fallback
(in-process, no forking) was used for AMIGA too.

v10.5 adds real concurrency: each session (inbound or outbound) now runs
as its own genuine AmigaOS process, spawned via CreateNewProcTags(). This
works because classic AmigaOS has one flat, shared address space -- no
fork()-style address-space isolation -- so a process spawned this way
sees the same globals, heap, and open library bases as its parent,
closer in practice to a thread than to a Unix fork(). An inbound
connection arriving mid-poll, or two outbound sessions whose schedules
happen to overlap, no longer have to wait their turn.

How many sessions can actually run at once is governed by the existing
"maxclients"/"maxservers" config keywords (see section 06) -- these
always existed in stock binkd but were never meaningfully exercised
before, since only one session ever ran regardless of their setting.

Nothing about how you configure or invoke AmiBinkD changes because of
this -- multiple "-P address" arguments, or a driver script invoking it
multiple times in sequence (section 09), work exactly as before. The
difference is purely that overlapping sessions no longer serialize.

This is worth knowing about before using "-P ALL" (added in v10.15, see
section 07): it makes every node in your config pollable in a single
run, so "maxclients" is what decides how many of them AmiBinkD calls at
the same time. Its default is 100, i.e. effectively all of them at once.
See section 06.

KNOWN, ACCEPTED LIMITATIONS OF THIS FIRST CONCURRENT RELEASE

* errno is a single global, shared by every concurrently-running
  session (classic AmigaOS again -- no per-process errno shadowing in
  this toolchain's C library). A retry/diagnostic path that reads errno
  right after a failed call could occasionally see a value a different,
  concurrently-running session's own call just set. This was thought
  rare in practice at the time this release shipped -- confirmed
  otherwise shortly after under a real burst of simultaneous inbound
  connections, and fixed (for the specific getpeername()/getsockname()
  critical section that raced) in v10.7. See v10.7's changelog entry and
  section 16 for what's still not covered.
* mypid (used in CRAM-MD5 challenge nonces) and rand()'s own internal
  state are likewise single shared globals across concurrent sessions.
  Nonces still combine with per-session timing/data, so this is a minor
  reduction in entropy variety between simultaneous sessions' nonces,
  not a security-relevant weakness.
* Shutdown while a session is still genuinely stuck (e.g. blocked
  indefinitely on a hung read) makes AmiBinkD wait rather than time out
  and exit anyway -- see section 12's entry on this. This is deliberate:
  a CreateNewProcTags(NP_Entry=...) child has no segment-list reference
  of its own to the code it's running, only the parent's does, so
  letting the parent's own exit() complete while a child was still
  running would risk the child executing out of memory that exit() had
  already freed. A wedged shutdown is recoverable (see section 12); a
  crash is worse.

True AmigaOS-native concurrency was the one open item in section 16's
"Known Limitations" this release actually closes.


===============================================================================
06. CONFIGURATION REFERENCE
===============================================================================

AmiBinkD uses the same config file format as stock binkd: one keyword
per line, "#" starts a comment, blank lines ignored. This section covers
only the keywords actually used in this port's own working configs --
stock binkd has additional keywords this setup never needed; consult
upstream binkd's own documentation for the complete list.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
domain <name> <outbound-path> <zone>
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Declares an FTN domain/network: its name, where its outbound flow files
live, and its zone number. One line per network you carry.

  domain cnet DH3:Echomail/Outbound/ 64

Alias form -- lets a hub/link refer to the same domain under another
name (case variants, alternate spellings):

  domain commodorenet alias-for cnet


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
address <ftn-address>@<domain>
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Your own FTN address within a domain. One line per domain/network.

  address 64:500/1@cnet


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
sysname / location / sysop
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Free-text strings sent to remote nodes during the handshake and shown in
your log.

  sysname "Reign of Fire BBS"
  location "Chattanooga, TN"
  sysop "Gary McCulloch"


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
nodeinfo
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Capability string advertised to remote nodes.

  nodeinfo 115200,TCP,BINKP


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
iport
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

TCP port for inbound connections (server mode).

  iport 24554

Leave this unchanged unless you have a specific reason to run on a
non-standard port and both sides agree.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
connect-timeout
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Seconds to wait for an outbound connect() to a hub/node to complete
before giving up. Defaults to 0 (disabled -- wait forever), same as
stock binkd on every platform.

  connect-timeout 60

HAS NO EFFECT ON AMIGA as of v10.11 -- v10.8 and v10.10 both tried to
implement it here (non-blocking socket + select(), then non-blocking
socket + a poll loop) and both failed live against a real remote: a
connection that had genuinely completed at the TCP level was never
recognized as connected by either technique, hanging the process
indefinitely regardless of this setting. Non-blocking connect() itself
doesn't reliably work on this bsdsocket_emu. Reverted to plain blocking
connect() -- see v10.11's changelog entry. Still set to 60 in all 8 of
this BBS's deployed configs as a harmless no-op, in case a future
toolchain/emulator fix makes it meaningful again; a genuinely
unresponsive remote is bounded only by the host's own underlying TCP
stack timeout now, not by this setting.

Note this is unrelated to hostname resolution, which happens before
connect() and is a separate matter -- see v10.9's, v10.13's, and v10.14's
changelog entries. As of v10.14, hostname resolution is a normal
gethostbyname() call again, same as every other platform this codebase
supports; no separate cache file or host-side script is involved.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
maxclients / maxservers / call-delay
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  maxclients 2
  maxservers 4
  call-delay 5

maxclients caps how many outbound sessions run at the same time;
maxservers does the same for inbound ones. Both default to 100. These
are stock binkd keywords that meant nothing on this port before v10.5
(only one session ever ran, whatever they were set to) and mean very
little with one-node-per-invocation polling either, since there is only
ever one node to call.

They matter as soon as you use "-P ALL" (section 07). Seven networks in
one invocation with the default maxclients means seven simultaneous
outbound sessions. That may well be fine; it is simply a different load
profile from the one-at-a-time driver-script pattern most setups grew
up on, and on a real 68k with modest RAM it is worth choosing
deliberately rather than inheriting. maxclients 2 is a reasonable
middle ground; maxclients 1 gives you strictly sequential polling
without needing separate scripts.

call-delay is how long the client manager waits before looking for more
work when maxclients sessions are already running. It defaults to 60,
which means a capped "-P ALL" run sits idle for a full minute between
each batch of calls. If you set maxclients low, set call-delay low too
-- 5 seconds is plenty.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
rescan-delay
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Minimum seconds between outbound-queue rescans.

  rescan-delay 1


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
send-if-pwd
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If present, AmiBinkD will only send (not just receive) files during a
session that authenticated with a password. A reasonable safety default
for inbound sessions from unconfigured/unknown addresses.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
log / loglevel / conlog
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  log SysData:log/AmiBinkD.log
  loglevel 4

log sets the logfile path. loglevel (1-9) sets verbosity. Level 4 is the
default and is meant to be readable without further tuning: one line per
connection, one per file transferred, one per result, plus the remote's
SYS name and FTN addresses. Level 5 and above add the full protocol
conversation -- the remote's greeting block (OPT/ZYZ/LOC/NDL/TIME/VER/
BUILD/TRF/QSIZE), mode negotiation, per-file `receiving'/`-> Inbound'
bookkeeping, connection attempts, and internal housekeeping such as
"downing clientmgr...". Level 7 adds the AmigaOS socket handoff trace.

  conlog 4

Uncomment/add conlog to also echo log output to the console/Shell
AmiBinkD was run from -- useful while testing interactively, noisy for
an unattended scheduled run.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
percents
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Print live transfer-progress percentages during send/receive. Cosmetic,
console/interactive-session only.

NOTE: this port's own deployment found that "printq" (list the queue
after each rescan) is safe to configure but was removed from this port's
production configs during troubleshooting as a diagnostic step -- it
was not actually the cause of anything and can be left enabled if you
want the extra queue-listing output. See section 15 if you're chasing a
different symptom and considering removing it again.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
backresolv
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Perform reverse DNS lookups for nicer hostnames in the log.
Cosmetic-only -- see section 15, finding 6, before enabling this if
you might receive inbound connections from a private/non-routable
address; it can hang an entire session on this port.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
inbound / inbound-nonsecure / temp-inbound
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  inbound DH3:Echomail/Inbound/
  inbound-nonsecure DH3:Echomail/Inbound/
  temp-inbound DH3:Echomail/Inbound_Temp/

Where received files land (inbound, for password-authenticated sessions;
inbound-nonsecure for unauthenticated ones -- can point at the same
directory), and where in-progress receives are staged before being
renamed into place (temp-inbound).


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
minfree / minfree-nonsecure
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  minfree 2048
  minfree-nonsecure 2048

Refuse new incoming files once free space (in KB) on the inbound
volume drops below this threshold.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
kill-dup-partial-files / kill-old-partial-files / kill-old-bsy
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  kill-dup-partial-files
  kill-old-partial-files 1d
  kill-old-bsy 2h

Housekeeping: remove a duplicate partial file when starting a fresh
receive; remove partial files older than the given age; remove stale
.bsy/.csy busy-flag files (normally left behind only by a crash or
abnormal exit) older than the given age. See section 15 for this port's
own finding about .bsy/.csy files -- kill-old-bsy does not appear to
clear the specific busy-file condition seen there, which resolves itself
each session regardless.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
nolog
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  nolog receiving*
  nolog *->*Inbound*

Suppress any log message matching a mask. Case-insensitive, matched
against the whole message text after formatting. Repeatable.

YOU PROBABLY DO NOT NEED THIS. At the default loglevel 4 the log is already
one line per connection, one per file and one per result -- the detail that
used to need masking (the remote's greeting block, mode negotiation, the
per-file `receiving'/`-> Inbound' bookkeeping, socket handoff) now sits at
level 5 and above and simply does not appear. `nolog' is for the case where
you have RAISED loglevel to chase something and want to keep one specific
message out of the way.

Use it to shape the log rather than editing message strings -- it needs no
rebuild, is reversible by commenting a line out, and keeps this port's
output identical to every other binkd so existing log tools still work.

TWO TRAPS, both learned the hard way:

  1. One mask per WORD. The parser adds every word on the line as its own
     mask, so "nolog receiving *" adds `receiving' AND `*' -- and `*'
     matches every message and silences the log completely. Masks must be
     single tokens. `*' spans spaces on its own, so "*->*Inbound*" still
     matches "x.pkt -> DH3:Echomail/Inbound/x.pkt".

  2. Masking hides your diagnostics too. If you have raised loglevel to
     investigate a stall or a socket leak, the messages you are about to
     mask are very likely the ones you raised it for. A mask makes a grep
     return zero, which reads as "no sessions" rather than "not logged".


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
set-file-dates
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  set-file-dates yes

Stamp received files with the sender's timestamp, and keep the datestamps
on our own .bsy/.csy busy flags fresh while a session runs.

DEFAULT ON THIS PORT: OFF. Every other binkd platform defaults it on, and
this is the one setting where AmiBinkD deliberately differs.

The reason is that setting a file's date on AmigaOS is SetFileDate(), and
when another Process holds the object that call does not fail -- it never
returns. There is no timeout to bound it and no watchdog on the session,
so a session that touches a file the BBS happens to be cataloguing at that
moment is simply gone: it keeps its server slot, its socket and its .bsy
locks forever. On the author's system, with C-Net/5's own overnight
file-catalog jobs running against the same directories, every single
inbound commit that reached that call hung -- and one of them landed
inside a poll client, which meant the BBS event that launched it never
finished and outbound mail stopped for seventeen hours.

What you give up by leaving it off is cosmetic: received files carry the
time they arrived rather than the time the sender created them. Nothing in
the BinkP protocol, in tossing, or in duplicate detection depends on it.

The one non-cosmetic use is the .bsy refresh, which stops a peer's
kill-old-bsy sweeping a lock out from under a session that is still
running. That only matters for a session lasting longer than the
kill-old-bsy age (2h in the sample config), which is far rarer than the
hang it avoids.

Turn it on only if you know your filesystem does not do this -- for
example a single-purpose machine where nothing else touches the inbound
and outbound directories while the mailer runs.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
aso
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Use Amiga-style outbound directory/filename conventions. Recommended for
this port -- it's what this port's own configs use and what has been
tested.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
node <address> <host>:<port> <password>
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  node 1:2/1@example your.hub.example.com:24554 YourAreafixPassword

Your uplink/hub for a given address: where to connect for outbound
polls, and the password (areafix/BinkP session password) both sides use
for CRAM-MD5 authentication. One line per node you poll or accept
authenticated mail from.

Keep real passwords out of anything you might publish or share --
amibinkd-example.cfg ships with placeholder values only.


===============================================================================
07. MULTI-NETWORK SETUP
===============================================================================

If you carry more than one FTN network, you have three supported
patterns (and can mix them):

1. One combined config with every domain/address/node line, polled with
   "-P ALL" -- one config, one command, every network (v10.15):

     AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -PALL AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD.cfg

   "ALL" is not case-sensitive, and works written either way ("-PALL"
   or "-P ALL"). AmiBinkD creates a poll for every node line in the
   config, skipping only nodes with no host to call and your own
   addresses, then polls them. This is the simplest pattern to
   maintain: adding a network is one node line, and config-wide changes
   (a new inbound path, a loglevel bump) are made once instead of once
   per network.

2. The same combined config, polled with one "-P" argument per network,
   when you want a specific subset rather than all of them:

     AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -P64:500/0 -P10:100/0 AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD.cfg

3. One config per network, each polled by its own invocation, chained
   from a driver script (see section 09):

     AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -P64:500/0 AmiBinkD:cnet.cfg
     AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -P10:100/0 AmiBinkD:araknet.cfg

   This is what this port's own deployment ran in production before
   v10.15, and it remains useful for polling one network by hand
   without disturbing the others. Its cost is duplication: seven
   networks means seven config files and seven scripts to keep in step.

All three are confirmed working, including real inbound file reception
and successful tosser import, across seven networks in one run.

Note the difference in timing between them. Patterns 1 and 2 hand every
requested node to a single running AmiBinkD, which will call up to
"maxclients" of them simultaneously (default 100 -- see sections 05 and
06). Pattern 3 runs one invocation per network, so its sessions are
serialized by the driver script itself regardless of any config
setting.

The combined config (AmiBinkD.cfg, with every domain/address/node line)
is also what the inbound server ("-s") should use, since it needs to
recognize every node that might call in, regardless of which pattern you
use for outbound polling. With pattern 1, the server and the client are
finally using the same single file.


===============================================================================
08. RUNNING THE PROGRAM
===============================================================================

Outbound poll, one address:

  AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -P<address> AmiBinkD:<config>

Outbound poll, several addresses in one run:

  AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -P<address1> -P<address2> AmiBinkD:<config>

Outbound poll, every node in the config (v10.15):

  AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -PALL AmiBinkD:<config>

The log records what "-P ALL" decided to do -- one "Polling <address>"
line per node at loglevel 5, then a summary at loglevel 3:

  ALL: created 7 poll(s)

If a node has no host to call, it is skipped rather than polled (a
poll file for it would never be acted on), and the summary says so:

  ALL: created 5 poll(s), skipped 2 node(s) with no host

Inbound server (stays running, listens for connections):

  AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -s AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD.cfg

A small watchdog script pattern -- check whether the server task is
already running under its expected console name, and start it if not --
is a reasonable way to keep the inbound server up across reboots without
starting a duplicate:

  STATUS <>NIL: COM=AmiBinkD
  IF WARN
    CD AmiBinkD:
    run <>NIL: AmiBinkD -s AmiBinkD.cfg WAIT QUIET
  ENDIF

Run this from your startup sequence, a scheduled event, or a periodic
maintenance script.


===============================================================================
09. DRIVER SCRIPTS (AMIGADOS EXECUTE PATTERN)
===============================================================================

A small AmigaDOS Execute script keeps the invocation simple to schedule
from a menu/event/maintenance command. With "-P ALL" (section 07,
pattern 1) one script covers every network -- this is amibinkd.scr,
included in the package:

  ; Poll every network in the config
  Stack 50000
  AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -PALL AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD.cfg

and the parent script that your event/maintenance schedule calls needs
only one entry:

  CD AmiBinkD:
  Execute amibinkd.scr
  Wait 1

For the per-network polling pattern (section 07, pattern 3), you write
one script per network instead:

  Stack 50000
  AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -P64:500/0 AmiBinkD:cnet.cfg

and the parent script chains them in sequence, one CD/Execute/Wait per
network:

  CD AmiBinkD:
  Execute cnet.scr
  Wait 1
  CD AmiBinkD:
  Execute araknet.scr
  Wait 1
  ...

That chain is also why the comment-character warning below is worth
reading: a single bad script aborts every network after it, too.

IMPORTANT: AmigaDOS Execute scripts use ";" for comments, not "#". If a
script has a "#"-prefixed comment line (for example, left over from a
Unix-shell-style template), Execute tries to run "#" as a literal,
nonexistent command, fails immediately with "Unknown command" / "failed
returncode 10", and -- because the default FAILAT threshold is 10 --
aborts not just that one script but the entire calling chain. This can
look exactly like a hang or a code-level bug in AmiBinkD itself; it is
neither. Always use ";" for comments in these scripts, and if a chained
poll run stops partway through with no further networks running, check
the very next script in the chain for a stray "#" line before looking
anywhere else.


===============================================================================
10. LOGGING
===============================================================================

AmiBinkD writes to the file configured by "log", at the verbosity set by
"loglevel". A typical successful outbound session logs, in order:

  BEGIN, ...
  creating a poll for <address> (`d' flavour)
  clientmgr started
  call to <address>
  trying <host> [<ip>]:<port>...
  connected
  outgoing session with <host>:<port> [<ip>]
  OPT CRAM-MD5-<challenge>
  Remote requests MD mode
  SYS / LOC / ZYZ / TIME / VER / BUILD lines
  addr: <address list from remote's AKA set>
  pwd protected session (MD5)
  QSIZE <n> files <n> bytes
  [receiving/rcvd/sending/sent lines for any files transferred]
  done (to <address>, OK, S/R: <sent>/<received> (<bytes>))
  session closed, quitting...
  the queue is empty, quitting...

A failed connection attempt (bad hostname, DNS not resolving, remote
down) logs a "getaddrinfo failed: ..." or connection-refused-style
message instead of "connected", followed by "done (to <address>,
failed, ...)".


===============================================================================
11. TESTING PROCEDURE
===============================================================================

Test an outbound poll:

1. Edit your config's "node" line with a real host/port/password for a
   node you control or that expects your test.
2. From a Shell:

     AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -P<address> AmiBinkD:<config>

3. Confirm the log shows "connected", a successful handshake, and
   "done (..., OK, ...)".

Test inbound (server mode):

1. Start the server: AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -s AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD.cfg
2. From another system (or another binkd instance), connect to your
   configured iport with a matching node password.
3. Confirm the log shows the incoming session completing, and that
   AmiBinkD returns to listening afterward (it should accept a second
   test connection without needing to be restarted).

Test multi-network polling:

1. Set up two or more networks per section 07.
2. Poll them with -P ALL, with multiple -P arguments in one invocation,
   or chained via driver scripts per section 09.
3. Confirm every network's session completes -- not just the first one.
   With -P ALL, check the "ALL: created N poll(s)" summary line first:
   if N is lower than the number of nodes you expected, the missing
   ones have no host to call and were skipped (see section 08). If the
   chain stops after the first network with no further output, see
   section 09's comment-character warning before assuming a code
   problem.

Test real mail flow, not just clean session logs:

1. Queue a real test message from another node addressed to you (or
   from your own system addressed outbound).
2. Poll (or wait for the server to receive it).
3. Confirm the .pkt file actually lands in your inbound directory and
   that your tosser processes it successfully -- a clean-looking BinkP
   session log does not by itself guarantee the received file was
   correctly finalized on disk; see section 15, finding 8, for why this
   distinction mattered on this port specifically.


===============================================================================
12. TROUBLESHOOTING
===============================================================================

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: getaddrinfo failed / Temporary failure in name resolution
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Check:

* The host:port in your "node" line -- typos are the most common cause
* Whether DNS is actually reachable from the Amiga/emulator's network
  stack at all
* Whether the address in "-P<address>" actually matches a configured
  "node" line for that domain -- a mismatched/mistyped address (e.g. a
  transposed digit) means AmiBinkD has no host to resolve at all


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: multi-network poll chain stops after the first network
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Check:

* Whether the next script in the chain has a "#"-prefixed comment line
  instead of ";" -- see section 09
* The log for that specific network -- did that session actually
  complete, or hang?
* Whether the chain is actually failing, versus just being slow (each
  session runs to completion before the next starts -- see section 05)


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: inbound server stops accepting connections after the first one
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is the class of bug this port fought hardest during development
(see section 15, findings 1-5). If you're running the exact build this
manual ships with, it should not recur -- but if you've modified the
socket/select handling, see section 15 in full before changing it
further; several of these bugs looked correct at the source level and
were only caught by live testing.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: "cannot rename ... No error!" in the log
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This was a real bug in early builds of this port (section 15, finding
8) -- a received file's rename-into-place step reported failure (with a
misleading "No error" message) even though the rename had actually
succeeded on disk, leaving the file stuck under a temp name in your
temp-inbound directory. Fixed as of this release. If you see this
message on a build newer than the fix, check whether your temp-inbound
and inbound directories are on the same AmigaDOS volume -- a genuine
cross-volume rename will still legitimately fail (AmigaDOS's Rename()
cannot move across volumes) and should be reported with a real, specific
errno rather than "No error", but a same-volume rename should not fail
at all on a fixed build.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: received files are missing / "missing tmp file" in the log
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This was a real bug in early builds of this port (section 15's
PRIuMAX/PRIdMAX note under "what changed" in the technical notes below)
caused by a format-string size mismatch corrupting the outgoing M_FILE
protocol message's byte-count/offset fields. Fixed as of this release.
If this recurs, it is worth checking the build's compiler flags match
what this port expects (-DHAVE_INTMAX_T in particular) rather than
assuming it's a fresh instance of the same root cause.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: "error unlinking '...csy': Text file busy" in the log
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Still not root-caused on this port -- see section 16. Usually cosmetic
(one busy-flag file per node, session still completes normally
afterward), but as of v10.3 it is confirmed capable of NOT clearing at
all: an ArakNet lock once stayed stuck for over 3 hours, hanging that
one poll and, since only one session runs at a time, blocking every
other configured network from being polled until the whole instance was
restarted. v10.3 bounds this: after 3 consecutive failed unlink
attempts for the same node, it backs off (holds that node for 5
minutes) instead of retrying forever, so a stuck lock can no longer
block the rest of the night's polling schedule. If the same node keeps
hitting this repeatedly, that is a signal worth investigating rather
than ignoring -- check for heavy concurrent file-write activity
elsewhere on the same drive image around the same time.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: AmiBinkD seems to hang instead of exiting (v10.5+)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected behaviour, not a bug, if a session is genuinely still active
(check the log for a session that never logged "done"/"session closed").
Since v10.5 (real concurrent sessions), shutdown deliberately waits
indefinitely for every in-flight session to finish rather than timing
out and exiting anyway -- see section 05's "Known, Accepted Limitations"
for why. You'll see a periodic "still waiting for N session(s) to
finish" log line (every ~10 seconds) rather than silence, so a wedged
shutdown is distinguishable from a genuinely frozen process. If a
session really is stuck (e.g. a remote that stopped responding
mid-transfer with no timeout ever tripping), the same recovery already
used for other stuck-process situations on this BBS applies: end the
whole Amiberry instance and relaunch it, same as recovering from any
other wedged Amiga-side process.

v10.8 and v10.10 both attempted a fix here (bounding connect() itself
with connect-timeout) and both failed live -- the real cause turned out
to be unrelated to timeouts entirely: outbound connect() runs in a
spawned child process that isn't the one that opened bsdsocket.library,
and a blocking connect()'s internal completion notification only
reaches whichever Process the library currently considers "the caller."
Fixed properly in v10.12 by giving each outbound-connecting child its
own private, unshared bsdsocket.library instance -- see v10.12's
changelog entry and section 05. connect-timeout still has no effect on
AMIGA (connect() is a plain blocking call again), but as of v10.12 that
should no longer matter in practice, since the connection itself should
now complete (or fail) within about a second, matching what a live
packet capture already proved the underlying TCP handshake does. If a
poll still hangs after "trying <host> [<ip>]..." under v10.12 or later,
that's a genuinely new, unexplained problem worth investigating fresh,
not a recurrence of this one.

A second cause, one step earlier, was originally worked around in v10.9
with a host-side DNS cache (a poll could hang inside hostname resolution
itself, before connect() was ever reached) and later confirmed fixed for
real by v10.12's private-bsdsocket.library-per-child fix -- see v10.9,
v10.13, and v10.14's changelog entries. As of v10.14 hostname resolution
is a plain gethostbyname() call again, no cache file or host-side script
involved. If a poll hangs with the log never even showing "trying <host>
[<ip>]...", that means hostname resolution itself is hanging again --
treat this as a serious regression and worth investigating fresh (check
first whether v10.12's private-SocketBase fix, client.c's call(), is
still intact) rather than assuming it's this same historical issue
recurring on its own.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Problem: session works from Shell but not from a scheduled event
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Check:

* Current directory / assigns available to the scheduled context
* Whether paths in the config are absolute rather than relying on a
  CD that only happens when run interactively
* Permissions on the config file, log directory, and outbound/inbound
  directories


===============================================================================
13. BEST PRACTICES
===============================================================================

* Test one node/network at a time before adding it to a scheduled chain
* Use real, distinct passwords per node -- don't reuse one password
  across every hub out of convenience
* Keep send-if-pwd enabled unless you specifically want to send mail to
  unauthenticated sessions
* Review logs regularly, especially after adding a new network
* Keep backups of your working config before editing it
* Test inbound (server mode) separately from outbound (poll mode) --
  they exercise different code paths
* If chaining multiple networks via driver scripts, test the full chain
  after adding or editing any one script -- a single bad line can abort
  the whole chain (see section 09)
* Don't enable backresolv unless you specifically want reverse-DNS
  hostnames in the log and understand the private-IP hang risk (section
  15, finding 6)


===============================================================================
14. SECURITY NOTES
===============================================================================

AmiBinkD accepts inbound TCP connections from the internet (or your
local network) and writes files to disk based on what the remote side
sends.

Recommended precautions:

* Set a real, per-node password for every configured node
* Use send-if-pwd so unauthenticated sessions can only receive from you,
  not pull your queued mail
* Don't point inbound/temp-inbound at directories your BBS or OS treats
  as auto-executed or otherwise sensitive
* Keep your config file's passwords out of anything you publish --
  amibinkd-example.cfg ships with placeholders only, on purpose
* Review logs regularly for unexpected connection attempts
* Keep backups


===============================================================================
15. REAL-HARDWARE FINDINGS (AMIBERRY BSDSOCKET_EMU)
===============================================================================

Every finding below compiled and linked fine, and looked correct from
the header/API surface alone -- each was only caught by actually running
this port live on real Amiberry. These are documented here because they
affect runtime *behavior*, not just this port's own source code -- if
you're maintaining or extending AmiBinkD (or writing other native
AmigaOS networking code against bsdsocket.library/bsdsocket_emu), check
this list before assuming unexpected behavior is a bug in your own code.

1. getaddrinfo()/getnameinfo() are not actually implemented by
   Amiberry's bsdsocket_emu, despite being declared as real
   bsdsocket.library vector calls. Calling them caused an immediate
   wild-jump crash. Worked around by using the classic
   gethostbyname()-based resolution path instead, never the "real"
   vector call.

2. ioctl(FIONBIO) / fcntl(O_NONBLOCK) do not work on bsdsocket socket
   descriptors -- they're AmigaDOS file-handle calls, and bsdsocket
   sockets aren't AmigaDOS file handles without ixemul's translation
   layer. They fail silently ("No such file or directory"), meaning a
   socket you thought you'd made non-blocking is still blocking.
   IoctlSocket() is bsdsocket.library's real equivalent -- use that
   instead.

3. A select()-ready listening socket's accept() is not guaranteed
   non-blocking, unlike real BSD sockets. accept() can block forever
   immediately after select() just reported that exact socket as ready,
   with no error and no crash -- just silence. Explicitly set the
   listening socket itself non-blocking (not just accepted session
   sockets), and treat EWOULDBLOCK/EAGAIN from accept() as a normal
   retry rather than a fatal error.

4. WaitSelect()'s "signals" parameter (for waking on Exec signals like
   SIGBREAKF_CTRL_C in addition to socket activity) does not work --
   passing it makes no observable difference; Ctrl-C can't interrupt a
   blocked select() call this way.

5. Calling WaitSelect() too rapidly breaks it. A tight polling loop
   (checking for Ctrl-C between short-timeout calls) eventually made
   WaitSelect() start returning -1 with errno left at 0 -- no real error
   condition, just a stuck function. When the caller already has a
   bounded timeout (the normal case), make exactly one WaitSelect() call
   per wait, matching normal call frequency, and check for Ctrl-C once
   afterward via SetSignal(0, mask) rather than polling in a loop. Only
   poll (in ~1 second steps) for the rarer case of wanting to block
   indefinitely.

6. Reverse DNS (backresolv) on a private/non-routable IP can hang an
   entire session. Not really an Amiberry-specific bug, but a real trap
   given this port's synchronous, one-session-at-a-time model (section
   05): an inbound connection from a LAN address triggers a synchronous
   reverse lookup that may never resolve, blocking everything (not just
   that session) until the remote side's own protocol timeout gives up
   first. backresolv only affects log cosmetics -- fine to leave
   disabled.

7. n_clients (a counter gating whether the client-mode poll loop is
   allowed to move on to the next queued node) was never decremented
   for the AMIGA build target in early builds of this port -- only for
   platforms with real threads or a DOS/DEBUGCHILD build. Invisible when
   polling a single address (nothing left to decrement for); polling
   more than one node in one invocation, or chaining several polls from
   a driver script, hung right after the first session's own "session
   closed, quitting..." log line, because the stale non-zero counter
   stopped the poll loop from ever re-evaluating the queue. Fixed in
   this release.

8. o_rename() (this port's AmigaOS Rename() wrapper, used to finalize a
   received file from its temp name to its real name) had its
   success/failure return value backwards in early builds of this port,
   and never set errno on the real failure path -- a bug in this port's
   own new code, not a bsdsocket_emu divergence, but just as invisible
   without live testing. AmigaDOS's Rename() returns *nonzero* on
   success (the standard AmigaDOS BOOL convention, same as Lock()/
   CreateDir()/DeleteFile()) -- the wrapper reported that as a POSIX
   failure and a real failure as POSIX success, inverted, with no
   errno set either way. The result: a rename that had already
   succeeded on disk got logged and treated as failed, silently
   orphaning received files under their temp names. Fixed in this
   release by inverting the return mapping and translating IoErr() to a
   real errno.


===============================================================================
16. KNOWN LIMITATIONS / NOT DONE YET
===============================================================================

* No zlib/bzip2 compression support (matches the historical Amiga binkd
  build, which also shipped without them).
* No DNS SRV-record lookup support (this toolchain lacks the resolver
  header it needs; the plain getaddrinfo()-based fallback covers every
  caller in practice).
* The piped external-transport feature (run3(), used by exactly one
  binkd feature) is stubbed to fail cleanly rather than implemented --
  not part of the core BinkP/FTN path.
* mypid and rand()'s internal state are shared globals across
  concurrently-running sessions (v10.5) rather than per-session -- see
  section 05's "Known, Accepted Limitations" for why this is low-risk
  in practice and not fixed this release. errno's exposure at the
  getpeername()/getsockname() critical section was fixed in v10.7; it
  remains a shared global at every other TCPERR()/TCPERRNO call site
  (client.c's outbound connect()/socket()/bind(), server.c's servmgr
  setup, iptools.c's ioctl paths) -- unconfirmed as an active problem
  there, but the same latent race in principle.
* backresolv (reverse/PTR lookups, getnameinfo()'s gethostbyaddr() call)
  is still disabled in all deployed configs, left that way as a
  precaution -- it uses the exact same class of bsdsocket.library call
  (from the same spawned, non-opener children) that v10.9's DNS hang and
  v10.12's connect() hang both turned out to share, and v10.12/v10.14
  together strongly suggest it would work fine now too, but this
  specific call path (reverse lookups on inbound sessions, including the
  long-lived persistent server) hasn't actually been re-tested live the
  way outbound gethostbyname() was in v10.13. Re-enabling it and
  watching a day's inbound traffic would be the natural next check if
  someone wants nicer hostnames in the log.
* bsdsocket_emu's UDP-socket support is now confirmed broken/unreliable
  on this Amiberry setup (v10.9 investigation) -- untested whether this
  affects anything else this port might someday want to use UDP for (it
  doesn't affect anything today; binkp itself is TCP-only), but worth
  keeping in mind before ever reaching for a UDP-based feature on this
  platform again.
* RESOLVED in v10.12, keeping this entry as a record of what looked
  right but wasn't: v10.8 and v10.10 both assumed the underlying problem
  was "how to detect connect() completion" (non-blocking + select(),
  then non-blocking + a re-issue-connect() poll loop) and both failed
  identically live against a real remote. The actual cause turned out to
  be nothing to do with blocking vs. non-blocking at all: outbound
  connect() runs in a branch()-spawned child that isn't the Process
  that opened bsdsocket.library, and a blocking connect()'s internal
  completion notification only reaches whichever Process the library
  currently associates as the caller. v10.12 gives each outbound child
  its own private, unshared bsdsocket.library instance instead, which
  sidesteps the whole per-Process-notification question. connect-timeout
  is a plain blocking call again as of v10.12 (no non-blocking machinery
  in client.c at all) and has no effect on AMIGA, same as v10.11 - not
  because it's broken, but because it was never the actual bottleneck.
* Soak testing to date covers one unattended overnight run (~7 hours,
  30-minute poll interval) across seven networks, under the old
  synchronous v10.4 model -- solid evidence against regressions in the
  bugs fixed through that release, but v10.5/v10.6/v10.7's concurrency has not
  yet had the same multi-day/high-volume soak treatment, and
  specifically has not yet been soak-tested with genuinely overlapping
  sessions (e.g. two networks polling at once) rather than just
  back-to-back ones -- see section 05.


===============================================================================
17. DIFFERENCES FROM STOCK UPSTREAM BINKD
===============================================================================

* Runs each BinkP session as a real AmigaOS process via
  CreateNewProcTags() rather than fork()/pthreads (neither exists on
  classic AmigaOS without ixemul.library) -- see section 05. Through
  v10.4 this build ran every session synchronously, one at a time;
  v10.5 added genuine concurrency.
* "-P ALL" is an addition, not an upstream feature: stock binkd's -P
  takes one FTN address per switch and has no way to say "every node in
  the config" (see sections 07 and 08). Any other value of -P behaves
  exactly as upstream, and "ALL" cannot collide with a real address
  since it isn't a valid Fido-style one.
* No ixemul.library/ixnet.library dependency at all -- the historical
  Amiga build of binkd required ixemul.library 47.0+; this port doesn't
  link against it or call any of its functions.
* Talks to bsdsocket.library directly via a small glue layer, rather
  than through ixemul's socket-emulation layer.
* getaddrinfo()/getnameinfo() always use the classic gethostbyname()-
  based emulation path on this build target, never bsdsocket.library's
  own (non-functional, on Amiberry) vector calls for those names -- see
  section 15, finding 1.
* No zlib/bzip2 compression and no DNS SRV-record lookups -- see section
  16.
* The piped external-transport feature (run3()) is stubbed rather than
  implemented -- see section 16.
* No double-precision floating point is used anywhere in this build; the
  handful of places stock binkd uses "double" (a live transfer-
  percentage counter, post-transfer CPS figures in log lines) were
  rewritten as integer/fixed-point math, because this toolchain's
  libgcc is missing the soft-float routines those would have needed. No
  user-visible behavior difference -- the same percentages and CPS
  figures are logged, just computed without floating point.

Everything else -- the BinkP protocol itself, FTN packet/outbound-flow
file handling, config file format and keyword semantics, and CRAM-MD5
authentication -- is unchanged from upstream binkd.


===============================================================================
18. VERSION HISTORY
===============================================================================

v10.31 - A Log You Can Read Without Editing It
---------------------------------------------

* At loglevel 4 a single received file cost three lines and one OPT exchange
  cost seven:

      - receiving 86be1d03.pkt (2249 byte(s), off 0)
      + 86be1d03.pkt -> DH3:Echomail/Inbound/86be1d03.pkt
      + rcvd: 86be1d03.pkt (2249, 2249.00 CPS)

  Measured over one night, the remote's greeting block alone (OPT, ZYZ, LOC,
  NDL, TIME, VER, BUILD, TRF, QSIZE) was 22% of the log -- all of it emitted
  by one Log() call in the M_NUL handler.

  Level 4 is now meant to be read as-is: one line per connection, one per
  file, one per result, plus the remote's SYS name and FTN addresses. The
  detail moved to level 5 and above, where raising loglevel brings it back.
  A 139-line poll window became 54.

* Removed AmiBinkD's own "handoff:" debug lines from normal view (now level
  7). Those trace the AmigaOS ReleaseSocket/ObtainSocket dance used to pass a
  socket to a child process. Upstream binkd forks and inherits the descriptor,
  so it has no equivalent message -- this port had been printing its own
  internals, including pointers and file descriptor numbers, into every
  sysop's log since v10.17.

* The benign .bsy unlink race is now level 5. It is a race between processes,
  not a fault, and nothing accumulates on disk -- but at level 4 it produced
  dozens of "could not remove own lock ... Permission denied" lines a night,
  which reads like a broken install.

* Because level 4 no longer needs trimming, the "nolog" masks are gone from
  the example config. "nolog" is unchanged and still documented (manual
  section 06) for masking a message once you have RAISED loglevel.

* Protocol and behaviour are untouched. Every change was a log level.


v10.30 - One Line Per Inbound Connection
----------------------------------------

* An inbound connection was announced twice, by two different processes:

      incoming from 72.58.128.97 (60539)
      Incoming: 72.58.128.97

  The first is kept and renamed -- it carries the port, which the second did
  not -- and the second is now outbound-only. Outbound output is unchanged.

  One consequence worth knowing: inbound peers are shown by IP rather than
  reverse-DNS name, because the accepting code resolves numerically on
  purpose. The session logs the remote's own SYS/ZYZ/LOC identity moments
  later, so the peer is not anonymous.


v10.26 to v10.29 - Session IDs and a Quieter Lock Race
------------------------------------------------------

* Every session logged the same id, so concurrent sessions could not be told
  apart in the log. Each session now logs its own AmigaOS task id.

  This is the shared-address-space trap that runs through this port: sessions
  are separate Processes but share ONE address space, so a file-scope static
  is shared by all of them. (v10.27 promptly reintroduced the same bug in a
  diagnostic and v10.29 removed it again.)

* Failing to remove our own .bsy lock is no longer reported as a fault when
  another process got there first -- that is the job done, not an error.



v10.25 - Log Lines Stop Being Shredded
--------------------------------------

* Log lines were being torn apart mid-write when two AmiBinkd instances ran
  at once. A real example:

      + 18 Aug 21:07:52 [1081963032] pwd protected session (MD5)
      nux/64                      <- fragment of "Linux/64"
      115                         <- fragment of "binkd/1.1a-115"

  Log() already took a lock, but a PRIVATE one. Upstream binkd is a single
  process with threads, so a private semaphore covers every writer it has.
  This port runs the inbound server and each poll as separate program
  invocations, so two or three instances write the same file with no lock
  between them.

  Log() now uses an Exec PUBLIC semaphore ("AmiBinkd.log"), which is the
  AmigaOS mechanism for locking across separate programs.

  NOTE: the fix only holds once EVERY instance is running v10.25. Replacing
  the binary is not enough on its own -- the long-running inbound server keeps
  the old code until AmigaOS restarts it, and a v10.24 server will still
  interleave with a v10.25 poll.

* Removed the "servmgr listen on *:24554" line. The port is already in the
  config, and the line cost width without adding anything.

* The startup banner now credits the port alongside the original author.


v10.24 - Outbound Mail Actually Leaves The System
-------------------------------------------------

* No outbound mail had ever left this port. Every bundle was sent as 0 bytes
  while a valid ZIP sat on disk containing the packet, and no layer logged an
  error because none had one: the tosser packed correctly and AmiBinkd sent
  exactly the byte count it was given.

  Cause: libnix13's fstat() always reports st_size == 0. It seeks to the
  start of the file, then measures with SEEK_CUR -- which can only return
  zero. It should use SEEK_END. fstat() returns success while doing so, so
  the caller gets a valid-looking struct describing an empty file.

  protocol.c's start_file_transfer() does fopen + fstat + use sb.st_size,
  identical to upstream binkd. amiga/fstat.c now overrides fstat(),
  re-measuring with SEEK_END and restoring the caller's file position.

  This affects any -mcrt=nix13 program that relies on file sizes, not just
  this one.

* SBTC_ERRNOPTR is now set on the shared SocketBase and on every private
  per-child base. Without it bsdsocket.library never writes to errno, yet
  iphdr.h defines TCPERR() as strerror(errno) on AMIGA -- so socket errors
  reported whatever unrelated call last touched errno, usually EACCES from a
  failed .bsy unlink. Socket errors now name real causes.

* pr_WindowPtr = -1 in main(), and NP_WindowPtr on spawned session Processes,
  so an AmigaOS "Please insert volume ..." requester can no longer block the
  mailer waiting for a human.

* Removing one of our own lock files no longer uses a 4-second blocking
  delete: ten bounded retries (~400ms), then log and move on. Stale-lock
  cleanup makes one non-blocking attempt. Poll times went ~14s -> 3-5s.

* libnix stdio's global ____filelist is guarded by a semaphore, since
  sessions are concurrent AmigaOS Processes sharing one address space.


v10.18 - Inbound Sessions Stop Hanging
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* Upgrade from v10.15, the previous public release. v10.16 and v10.17
  were never released; they are listed below because they explain the
  version jump and because the AmigaOS problems they uncovered are worth
  passing on. Nothing shipped between v10.15 and this release.

* Root cause of the whole v10.16-v10.18 arc was setting a file's
  datestamp. On AmigaOS that is SetFileDate(), and when another Process
  holds the object it does not fail -- it never returns. Nothing bounds
  it and nothing watches the session, so the session is lost along with
  its server slot, socket and .bsy locks. Accumulate enough and the
  server reaches "maxservers" and refuses all inbound.

  It only triggers when something else touches the same directories,
  which is why it presented as a night-time-only fault: on the author's
  system 66 of 66 inbound commits completed during the day and 7 of 7
  hung after 21:00, when C-Net/5's own file-catalog jobs run. One hang
  landed inside a poll client, so the BBS event that started it never
  finished and outbound mail stopped for seventeen hours.

* Fixed by the new "set-file-dates" setting (section 06), which defaults
  OFF on this port -- the one place AmiBinkD deliberately differs from
  every other binkd platform. The cost is cosmetic: received files carry
  their arrival time rather than the sender's.

* Verified over 18 hours spanning the window that broke v10.17: 89
  inbound sessions started and 89 closed with nothing leaked, 351 file
  commits, session count peaking at 5 and returning to zero between
  polls, 59 of 59 scheduled mail events completing. v10.16 saturated in
  13 hours; v10.17 had leaked 55 sessions by 26 hours.

v10.17 - One Hung Session No Longer Takes The Others With It (unreleased)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* Never released; superseded by v10.18. Refreshing .bsy datestamps happens on every pass
  of the protocol main loop, and that work was done while holding a
  single global lock across file I/O -- so one session blocked in there
  pinned the lock and every other concurrent session piled up behind it,
  a pile-up that fed itself. v10.17 removed the cascade; v10.18 removed
  the hanging call.

v10.16 - Inbound Socket Handoff (unreleased; fix retained in v10.18)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* Never released. Its inbound fix was real and is retained, but on test
  it traded one failure for another: hung sessions
  leaked permanently and accumulated until inbound stopped, which in
  practice was worse than v10.15's quieter failure. 107 of 128 sessions
  leaked in twelve hours on the author's system, and their .bsy locks
  stopped the BBS poll script before it could launch the mailer --
  eleven hours with no outbound mail and only "error: 8" in the event
  log. That leak is fixed in v10.18 and the socket handoff below is
  retained. Notes kept because the underlying problem is instructive for
  anyone porting to AmigaOS.

* Applies to any mailer, not just this one: if your event script deletes
  .bsy/.csy before polling, a failed delete must not abort the script. On
  AmigaDOS use "FAILAT 21" before those deletes and "FAILAT 10" after. A
  lock held by a running session will otherwise kill the whole event.
  "kill-old-bsy" (section 06) already sweeps stale locks.

* The original v10.16 notes follow, for reference only:

* Inbound BinkP sessions never worked in any release from v10.5 through
  v10.15.

  What you would have seen: the log records

      + <date> incoming session with <peer>

  and then nothing more for that session -- no error, no timeout, no
  close -- while the calling system reports "Session timeout" and
  "Authorization failed". Because the stuck session never released its
  server slot, the next caller was refused outright, so inbound mail
  stopped within a few minutes of every startup and a restart looked
  like it helped. Outbound polling was entirely unaffected, so mail you
  collected yourself still arrived normally, which made the fault easy
  to attribute to the remote system rather than to AmiBinkD.

  Cause: on AmigaOS each Process gets its own bsdsocket.library context,
  and socket readiness is delivered by signal to the Process the library
  regards as the caller. Since v10.5 each session runs as its own
  Process (section 05), but inbound sessions kept using the parent's
  shared library base for a socket they did not own, so those readiness
  signals never reached them. The session could therefore neither send
  nor receive -- it had queued its greeting but never put a byte on the
  wire -- and simply waited forever. v10.12 fixed this same class of
  problem for outbound connections; inbound was left uncovered.

  AmiBinkD now transfers the accepted socket into the session's own
  private library base using ReleaseSocket()/ObtainSocket(), which is
  bsdsocket.library's documented mechanism for passing a socket between
  Processes. See section 15 if you maintain this on another TCP/IP
  stack -- the transfer is standard and not Amiberry-specific.

* Also fixed by the same change: the "timeout" keyword (section 06) had
  no effect on stalled inbound sessions, which could linger for tens of
  minutes. That timeout is driven by the same socket-readiness loop, so
  it now works as documented. No configuration change is required.

* Note: do not set "maxservers" as a workaround for the old symptom. On
  this port a rejection can take the server manager down with it,
  stopping inbound entirely. Leave it unset (default 100).

* Verified live: five consecutive inbound sessions from a network hub in
  44 seconds -- full handshake, CRAM-MD5 authentication, packets
  received into the inbound directory, clean teardown each time, and the
  listener still accepting afterwards. Outbound polling unchanged over
  the same period.

v10.15 - Poll Every Network From One Config ("-P ALL"), Custom Icon
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* New: "-P ALL" polls every node in the config in a single invocation
  (sections 07, 08 and 09):

    AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD -p -PALL AmiBinkD:AmiBinkD.cfg

  Stock binkd's -P takes one FTN address per switch, which left two
  ways to carry several networks: repeat -P once per uplink, or keep a
  separate config and driver script for each. The second is what this
  port's own deployment did -- seven networks meant seven .cfg files
  and seven .scr files to keep in step, and every config-wide change
  had to be made seven times. "-P ALL" removes that: one config, one
  command line. The inbound server ("-s") already used the combined
  config, so the client side now uses the same single file.
* "ALL" is matched case-insensitively and accepted in either form
  ("-PALL" or "-P ALL"). It cannot collide with a real -P argument,
  since it isn't a valid Fido-style address -- before this release the
  same command line simply logged "`ALL' cannot be parsed as a
  Fido-style address" and polled nothing.
* Two kinds of node are deliberately skipped rather than polled: nodes
  with no host to call (hosts unset or "-"), because the queue would
  never act on such a poll and the outbound would just accumulate
  orphan .dlo files; and your own addresses, in case one is also listed
  as a node line. Each skip is logged at loglevel 4 and counted in the
  loglevel-3 summary ("ALL: created 5 poll(s), skipped 2 node(s) with
  no host").
* Implementation note for anyone reading the source: poll_all_nodes()
  in ftnnode.c, dispatched from binkd.c's poll-creation loop, walks the
  node array with the existing foreach_node() and calls the same
  create_poll() that a normal -P does. It is the same per-node work as
  poll_node(), minus the address parsing -- not a separate polling path
  with its own behavior.
* Worth setting alongside this: "maxclients" (and "call-delay") now
  actually decide something. With every uplink pollable in one run,
  the default maxclients of 100 means every network is called
  simultaneously, where the per-script pattern was strictly one at a
  time. See section 06; this BBS's own config uses maxclients 2 with
  call-delay 5.
* Confirmed live on the deployment this port is developed against:
  a scheduled poll cycle logged "ALL: created 7 poll(s)" and completed
  clean sessions with all seven networks, two at a time, including real
  inbound file reception.

Also in this release -- the packaging work 10.15 was first numbered for:

* Replaced DH4:AmiBinkD/AmiBinkD.info, previously a reused copy of the
  RoFTIC icon (byte-identical, same file), with a purpose-made one: the
  Reign of Fire dragon-head badge cropped to just its circular emblem,
  quantized to a 64-colour palette-mapped image, and alpha-masked to a
  circle so it sits cleanly on the Workbench desktop instead of
  carrying a black square background. A distinct, brighter/hotter
  "selected" image is shown while the icon is clicked, instead of
  whatever the reused RoFTIC icon's own selected state happened to be.
* Built via icon.library's own V44+ API (NewDiskObject/IconControlA/
  PutIconTagList) rather than a hand-rolled on-disk format - reverse
  engineering the existing icon's on-disk FORM ICON encoding (a real
  compressed IFF FACE/IMAG structure, confirmed by walking the chunks
  of the reused RoFTIC icon and the AmigaOS 3.2 NDK's icon.doc/icon.h)
  turned out to be unnecessary and risky to hand-roll correctly; letting
  the OS's own code write the file sidesteps that entirely. The tooling
  lives in ~/AmiBinkD-icon-tool/: gen_icon_data.py crops/quantizes the
  source artwork into icon_data.h (palette + chunky pixel arrays for
  both the normal and selected states, circular alpha mask baked in),
  and buildicon.c (cross-compiled with the same amiga-gcc toolchain as
  AmiBinkD itself, using the newer NDK headers since icon.library V44
  needs AmigaOS 3.5+) calls the real icon.library API to write
  AmiBinkD.info. Re-run both any time the source artwork changes.
* Requires AmigaOS 3.5+ (icon.library V44 or later) to render the
  colour image - matches this system, which is already running AmigaOS
  3.2. Older Workbench versions fall back to whatever default/generic
  icon they'd show for a WBTOOL with no readable colour extension.
* The icon work alone was briefly released as a packaging-only 10.15
  with the v10.14 binary. "-P ALL" landed the following morning and was
  folded into the same version number rather than becoming 10.16,
  specifically so 10.15 doesn't sit in this history as a version nobody
  can point at a feature for. If you have an AmiBinkD10_15 archive
  whose binary reports v10.14 at startup, that is the short-lived
  earlier cut -- replace it with this one.

v10.14 - DNS Cache Mechanism Removed For Good
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* v10.13's experiment (see that changelog entry) is confirmed: 2 full
  days, 2 reboots, ~60 poll cycles per network across all 7 networks,
  zero recurring failures (one isolated, non-reproducing blip on one
  boot, never seen again on the second reboot or since). gethostbyname()
  genuinely works now, including on the original problem hub
  (AmigaNet) - v10.12's private-bsdsocket.library-per-outbound-child fix
  fixed this hang too, as a side effect, exactly as suspected.
* Removed the v10.9 host-side DNS cache mechanism entirely: the
  cache-lookup function is gone from rfc2553.c (getaddrinfo() just
  calls gethostbyname() directly again, same as every other platform
  this codebase supports, with the numeric-address short-circuit kept -
  it's a legitimate optimization on its own), the
  ~/amibinkd-dns/refresh.py script and its systemd --user timer/service
  are deleted, and the stale DH0:AmiBinkd/dns_cache.txt file is removed.
  Don't reintroduce this class of workaround without new evidence
  gethostbyname() is broken again - and check whether v10.12's
  private-SocketBase fix is still in place first if it ever does
  resurface, since that's what actually fixed the root cause.
* This also clears the blocker on refreshing the DH4:AmiBinkD/
  redistributable package (see v10.9's changelog entry and manual.txt's
  earlier notes on this) - the package no longer depends on any
  Reign-of-Fire-specific host-side infrastructure to resolve hostnames.
  The package refresh itself is a separate, not-yet-done task.
* Deployed to DH0:AmiBinkd/AmiBinkd (v10.13 kept as
  AmiBinkd.v10.13-backup).

v10.13 - EXPERIMENTAL: Testing Whether The DNS Cache Is Still Needed
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* v10.9's cache-only DNS lookup (see that changelog entry) was built to
  work around gethostbyname() hanging on this bsdsocket_emu - but at the
  time, the *why* wasn't understood, only that it hung. v10.12 later
  found the real cause: spawned outbound children never received
  connect()-completion notifications because they weren't the Process
  that opened bsdsocket.library, fixed by giving each one its own
  private library instance - confirmed live across all 7 networks plus
  a clean overnight soak (14/14 poll cycles, zero failures).
* gethostbyname() is the same class of bsdsocket.library call, from the
  same spawned children, as the connect() calls v10.12 fixed. Plausible
  v10.12 fixed this hang too, as a side effect - which would make the
  whole host-side DNS cache script (~/amibinkd-dns/refresh.py + its
  systemd timer, external to this package, never shipped with it)
  unnecessary. That mechanism was also this port's biggest problem for
  redistribution: anyone downloading the package without replicating
  Reign of Fire's own host-side infrastructure would get permanent,
  silent DNS failures on any hostname-based node line.
* Testing directly: getaddrinfo() (AMIGA build) now calls gethostbyname()
  again for non-numeric hostnames - the numeric-address short-circuit
  added in v10.9 stays (still correct regardless of which path handles
  the non-numeric case). The systemd timer is stopped and disabled; the
  cache-lookup function stays defined in rfc2553.c but unused, for a
  fast revert if needed. Running this against a full day of real
  scheduled traffic across all 7 networks to see whether it holds.
* If this holds: the cache mechanism and its host-side script can be
  removed for good in a future release, and the redistributable package
  refresh (paused as of v10.12 specifically because of this gap) can
  resume. If gethostbyname() hangs again: revert to
  amiga_dns_cache_lookup() and re-enable the systemd timer - don't reach
  for a third mechanism first.

v10.12 - Real Fix: Private bsdsocket.library Base Per Outbound Session
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* v10.11's revert turned out not to fix the underlying bug, and a live
  packet capture finally proved why. Captured an actual poll attempt at
  the wire level: TCP handshake completes in well under a second every
  time, the remote's BinkP handshake data (227 bytes) arrives fully ACKed
  at the kernel level within another second - and AmiBinkD's own process
  still never logs "connected," never reads the data, and does nothing
  until externally interrupted. Also discovered this was never specific
  to one hub: the user confirmed every configured network hung the same
  way, and a different AmigaOS FTN mailer on the same machine (FidoBlitz)
  connects and polls successfully with no issue.
* Root cause: since v10.5, every outbound connection attempt runs inside
  a spawned CreateNewProcTags child (client.c's do_client() ->
  branch(call, ...)) - a different Process from the one that actually
  opened bsdsocket.library (amiga_glue.c's amiga_socket_init(), called
  once in the top-level process). That function's own v10.5-era comment
  already documented the relevant SBTC_CAN_SHARE_LIBRARY_BASES tradeoff
  ("SBTC_SIGIOMASK-style per-Process signal delivery only works for
  whichever Process last configured it") but reasoned only about
  select() (already bounded-polling here, not signal-wait). What that
  reasoning missed: a *blocking* connect() call's own internal
  completion notification likely depends on this exact same per-Process
  delivery mechanism (libraries/bsdsocket.h documents real
  SBTC_BREAKMASK/SIGIOMASK/SIGURGMASK/SIGEVENTMASK Task-notification
  tags) - so the wakeup for a spawned, non-opener child's connect()
  never arrives, regardless of blocking, non-blocking+select() (v10.8),
  or non-blocking+poll (v10.10) - all three fail the same way because
  none of them change *which Process gets notified*. This also explains
  why inbound sessions (server.c's spawned children) work fine: their
  whole I/O path uses non-blocking sockets + bounded select(), which
  never depended on this notification mechanism in the first place -
  connect() was the one remaining blocking, library-internal call in a
  non-opener child.
* Fixed by giving each outbound-connecting child its own private,
  unshared bsdsocket.library instance for its whole session lifetime -
  matching how FidoBlitz and pre-v10.5 AmiBinkD both worked - without
  touching the shared SocketBase every other concurrently-running
  Process (top-level clientmgr/servmgr, inbound session children) still
  depends on. Mechanism: bsdsocket.library's ~40 call-site macros
  (socket(), connect(), send(), select(), gethostbyname(), etc.) all
  resolve their library base through one macro, BSDSOCKET_BASE_NAME.
  Redefining it to a function call instead of a bare global -
  amiga_current_socketbase(), which returns the calling Task's own
  private base (stashed in tc_UserData) if it has one, or falls back to
  the existing shared SocketBase otherwise - gives every call site
  correct, per-Task resolution automatically, with no changes needed at
  any individual call site anywhere in the codebase. client.c's call()
  (the whole branch()-spawned entry point, not just the connect() line)
  now opens a private base via amiga_open_private_socketbase() at entry
  and closes it via amiga_close_private_socketbase() before returning;
  degrades to the shared base (today's still-broken behaviour) rather
  than aborting the poll if the open fails.
* Required a companion fix in branch.c: amiga_proc_trampoline() freed
  its transient argument-handoff struct but never reset tc_UserData
  afterward, leaving every freshly spawned child (not just outbound
  ones) with a dangling pointer where the new per-Task lookup needed a
  safe NULL default. Now explicitly reset to NULL right after the free.
* Deployed to DH0:AmiBinkd/AmiBinkd (v10.11 kept as
  AmiBinkd.v10.11-backup). CONFIRMED LIVE the same day: a poll to
  39:902/0@amiganet logged "connected" 1 second after "trying ...",
  then completed a full session and closed cleanly -
  "done (to 39:902/0@amiganet, OK, S/R: 0/2 (0/7773 bytes))" -
  the first successful poll to this hub across the entire v10.8-v10.12
  investigation. This is the real fix.

v10.11 - Reverted To Plain Blocking connect() On AMIGA
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

* v10.10 shipped believing it had fixed connect()-completion detection
  by replacing select()/WaitSelect() with a re-issue-connect() poll
  loop. It hadn't. The very next real test against
  hub.bottomlessabyss.net hung exactly the same way v10.8's original
  code did: a connection that had genuinely completed at the TCP level
  (host-side socket state showed CLOSE-WAIT with the remote's reply
  already sitting unread) was never recognized as connected.
* This ruled out the v10.10 diagnosis. v10.10's timeout bound was a
  plain local counter, not dependent on select()/WaitSelect() or the
  emulator's cooperation in any way - and it still never fired. The
  only way that's possible is if the individual connect() calls inside
  the poll loop were themselves blocking for extended periods, despite
  IoctlSocket(FIONBIO) reporting success beforehand. Conclusion:
  non-blocking connect() itself doesn't reliably work on this
  bsdsocket_emu - not just one particular technique for polling its
  completion (select(), and now repeated connect() calls, have both
  failed identically).
* Also worth naming plainly: it's possible a standalone "connect() to
  an unresponsive remote hangs forever" bug never actually existed on
  its own here. The live incident that originally motivated v10.8 was
